prompt: In the TAP report of the first run, which line tells a pipeline to go red?
hint: A pipeline does not read the report at all.

choices.text: not ok 4
choices.why: That line is for people; a pipeline does not parse it to decide.

choices.text: # fail 1
choices.why: The summary says the same thing in words, and a pipeline still does not read it.

choices.text: None: it reads the exit code, 1
choices.why: Right. echo $? printed 1, and that is what a CI step checks.

choices.text: TAP version 13
choices.why: That only names the format.

prompt: Why does the HEAD test get the todo option instead of being deleted?
hint: What happens to the defect, and to the run?

choices.text: A todo test is skipped, so it costs nothing
choices.why: A todo test still runs; its result is reported and only its failure does not count.

choices.text: The run stays green and the defect stays in the report
choices.why: Right. Deleting it would lose the defect; leaving it red teaches people to ignore red.

choices.text: Node refuses to run a test that has failed twice in a row
choices.why: Node keeps no history of earlier runs.

choices.text: boxoffice will fix itself once the defect is reported in TAP
choices.why: Nothing reads the TAP file back into boxoffice; a person has to fix the code.

prompt: A test compares price_cents with assert.equal from node:assert/strict, and boxoffice sends "6500" as a string. What happens?
hint: Which comparison does the strict variant use?

choices.text: It passes, because the two print the same
choices.why: Looking the same is the loose comparison; strict uses ===.

choices.text: It passes, because JSON has only one kind of number
choices.why: "6500" in JSON is a string, not a number.

choices.text: It throws before the comparison, while reading the body
choices.why: The body is valid JSON; reading it works.

choices.text: It fails: '6500' is not 6500 under ===
choices.why: Right. That is why the lesson uses the strict variant.

prompt: Why does payments.test.mjs read the stub's /__requests after placing an order?
hint: What does boxoffice's 201 not prove?

choices.text: To get the order's id, which boxoffice does not return
choices.why: boxoffice returns the id in the body; the test reads it there.

choices.text: To check the other side: one charge, for the right amount
choices.why: Right. A perfect 201 can hide a missing or doubled charge.

choices.text: To make the stub approve the next charge
choices.why: Reading the record changes nothing; PUT /__mode sets the mode.

choices.text: Because boxoffice cannot answer until the stub is read
choices.why: boxoffice answered before the test read anything.

prompt: Match each hook in payments.test.mjs to what it does.
hint: One runs before every test.

pairs.right: gets one token for the whole file
empties the stub's record and sets it to approve
leaves the stub approving for whoever comes next

right_distractors: restarts boxoffice so sh-102 is full again

prompt: Someone removes the after hook from payments.test.mjs. Which failure becomes possible?
hint: What mode is the stub in when the last test finishes?

choices.text: The second test of this file fails, because the token expired
choices.why: The token lives fifteen minutes and is not touched by after.

choices.text: boxoffice keeps the declined order and runs out of seats
choices.why: A declined order holds no seats.

choices.text: Another file's test meets a stub still in decline mode
choices.why: Right. The last test sets decline, and only after puts approve back.

choices.text: None, because beforeEach runs after the last test as well
choices.why: beforeEach runs before each test of this file and never after the last.

prompt: The first version of seats.test.mjs passed, then failed on a second run against the same boxoffice. Why?
hint: Read the failure, 0 !== 2.

choices.text: The first run had already sold two of the four seats
choices.why: Right. The test assumed it was the first thing to happen to sh-103.

choices.text: Node caches results and reports the cached one
choices.why: Node reruns every test; the 0 came from boxoffice.

choices.text: The token from the first run had been revoked
choices.why: The failure is about seats_left, not a 401.

choices.text: It is flaky, and a third run would pass if you simply tried again
choices.why: A third run would fail the same way, with 409 this time; nothing about it is random.

prompt: Swapping the two file names on the command line did not change which test failed. Why not?
hint: Look at the order of ok and not ok in both runs.

choices.text: --test-concurrency=1 runs the files at the same time
choices.why: It runs them one at a time, which is why the order is fixed.

choices.text: boxoffice was not restarted between the runs
choices.why: It was restarted, and the same test still failed.

choices.text: node sorts the files, so seats runs first either way
choices.why: Right. The order is an accident of the names.

choices.text: The sellout test always fails, alone or not
choices.why: It passed alone against a fresh boxoffice.

prompt: Why does the lesson fix the two tests with a server per file instead of unique data per test?
hint: What would unique data mean here?

choices.text: Unique data is slower than starting a server
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the remedy is simply not available.

choices.text: boxoffice cannot create a show of the test's own
choices.why: Right. Three fixed shows leave nothing unique to create.

choices.text: Unique data would need a database, and boxoffice has none
choices.why: Unique data needs a way to create things; memory would do if boxoffice offered it.

choices.text: Node cannot run two tests that use different shows
choices.why: Node runs any number of tests on anything.

prompt: To run test files one at a time instead of in parallel, node --test takes the option --test-___=1.
hint: It counts how many run at once.

prompt: Why is a fixed one-second sleep before reading the report a poor fix?
hint: Two problems, at both ends.

choices.text: Node has no way to sleep inside a test
choices.why: setTimeout works in a test; eventually uses it.

choices.text: The report never updates while a test is sleeping
choices.why: It updates on boxoffice's own timer, test or no test.

choices.text: Slow on every run, and still too short on a busy machine
choices.why: Right. A deadline with polling avoids both.

choices.text: A sleep makes the test pass even when the report is wrong
choices.why: The assertion after the sleep still checks the values.

prompt: When eventually runs out of time, it throws the last assertion error rather than a "timed out" message. What does that give the reader?
hint: Look at the failure with REPORT_DELAY=5000.

choices.text: Which fields were wrong, and what they held
choices.why: Right. The diff showed zeros against 1, 3 and 24000.

choices.text: A faster failure, since the deadline is skipped
choices.why: The deadline is kept; the duration was over three seconds.

choices.text: A pass, since the last attempt is the one counted
choices.why: The last attempt failed, so the test failed.

choices.text: The value of REPORT_DELAY that boxoffice used
choices.why: Nothing in the error names the delay; the reader has to know it.

prompt: Right after the order of three seats, how many orders did the sales report show?
hint: The report lags behind.

prompt: Why does run-integration.sh refuse to start when something already answers on port 8080?
hint: Who would answer the health check?

choices.text: Two servers on one port would split the requests between them
choices.why: Only one process can listen on a port; the second exits with EADDRINUSE.

choices.text: An old server would answer while the new one died
choices.why: Right. The tests would then run against a server with an unknown history.

choices.text: curl cannot reach a port another program opened
choices.why: curl reached it; that is how the check found it.

choices.text: The trap would kill the old server and lose its data
choices.why: trap kills only the pids the script started.

prompt: Put what run-integration.sh does in order.
hint: Dependencies first, and nothing goes on before an answer.
items: check that ports 8080 and 8090 are free

prompt: Why does the script name 'tests/*.test.mjs' instead of running node --test with no file at all?
hint: Lesson 8 left a file in the project.

choices.text: Without a file, node --test refuses to start
choices.why: With no file it searches the directory with its default patterns.

choices.text: The glob makes the files run one at a time
choices.why: Concurrency is a separate option; the glob only chooses files.

choices.text: Node's default search skips the tests directory
choices.why: It would find tests/*.test.mjs; the trouble is what else it finds.

choices.text: The default search also takes karate-config.js under src/test
choices.why: Right. Any .js under a directory named test counts as a test file.

prompt: A colleague's suite passes on their laptop and fails on CI one run in four, always in a test that reads seats_left of sh-103 from the shared boxoffice. What do you suspect first?
hint: What differs between a laptop and a CI runner, and who else touches sh-103?

choices.text: A network problem on the CI runner, worth retrying the job
choices.why: A network problem would hit every test, not one that reads shared seats.

choices.text: Another file buying sh-103 seats in parallel
choices.why: Right. Shared state plus parallel files gives a result that depends on timing.

choices.text: A different Node version on CI that counts seats differently
choices.why: Seats are counted by boxoffice, the same code on both machines.

choices.text: The report lag of REPORT_DELAY
choices.why: seats_left is computed at once from the orders; only the sales report lags.

prompt: Which of these would make report.test.mjs pass by luck, or fail at random, rather than by what boxoffice does?
hint: Think of where its report could get orders from, and of fixed waits.

choices.text: Using the shared boxoffice on 8080 instead of its own on 8183
choices.why: Right. Other files' orders would reach the same report and change the totals.

choices.text: Replacing eventually with a sleep of 600 ms
choices.why: Right. On a busy runner the rebuild can take longer, and the test fails at random.

choices.text: Asserting all three fields with deepEqual
choices.why: Exact values are right here, because the test owns the only orders.

choices.text: Stopping its boxoffice in after
choices.why: Stopping it is what keeps the next run clean.

prompt: Match each symptom to the cause this lesson showed for it.
hint: Four sections, four causes.

pairs.left: a test passes alone and fails in the suite
the report shows zeros right after an order
pairs.right: the report is rebuilt REPORT_DELAY later

pairs.left: curl: 7 on the first request of a script
pairs.right: the server was not listening yet

pairs.left: a decline test is followed by unexpected 402s elsewhere
pairs.right: the stub was left in decline mode

right_distractors: the token expired between two tests

prompt: The sales report becomes a separate service fed by a queue, and it may take up to ten seconds to catch up. What should change in report.test.mjs?
hint: The shape of the test is right; one number is not.

choices.text: Replace eventually with a sleep of ten seconds
choices.why: Every run would pay ten seconds, and a slower day would still fail.

choices.text: Drop the assertion on the report, since a queue is not testable
choices.why: That turns a real promise into something no test holds.

choices.text: Raise eventually's timeout above ten seconds
choices.why: Right. It still returns as soon as the report agrees, so a fast run stays fast.

choices.text: Lower the polling interval to one millisecond
choices.why: Asking more often does not make the report arrive sooner; the deadline is what is too short.
